blocks.text: MS NICOLA DENNISON (sworn)
Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
Could we start with your full name, please?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Nicola Anne Dennison.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: And your occupation, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Nursery nurse at the neonatal unit, Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Were you employed in that capacity in November 2015?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: How long have you, as a matter of interest, been employed at the NNU at Chester?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Since 1985, barring a couple of years.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Right, thank you. We've heard that nurses are given bands by way of categorisation.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: What band are you and would you have been in November 2015?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm a band 4 and I'm a nursery nurse, not a registered nurse.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Thank you. You've been asked about your involvement with a baby named [Baby J], back in November 2015. Did you complete a series of night shifts towards the end of that particular month?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: And did you care for [Baby J] on those night shifts?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Do you have a recollection of [Baby J]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I do.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: What do you remember about [Baby J]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She was a nice little baby. She was lively, she was alert, she was engaging. She also had medical concerns, which is unusual for our unit. She had stomas, she had a Broviac line, and as a band 4 it was unusual for us to look after that, but she was a well baby going home with those medical conditions, so was at that point of almost being ready for home.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Right. We've heard a little bit about stomas and Broviac lines. Did you have experience of stomas and Broviac lines?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Were you comfortable dealing with both of those features?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I was. Can I clarify though that we didn't do anything with the Broviac line, it was just present.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: That was cared for once a week on Friday and that was dealt with registered members of staff.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Thank you. That's a Broviac line --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's the Broviac --
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: I think the stoma (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The stoma needed regular care. Feeds every 3 hours and that was a normal part of her care and was going to be a normal part of her parental care at home.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Okay. With that in mind, at the stage that we are discussing, at the end of November, were her parents involved in her stoma care and her cares generally?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, during the day when they were present on the unit.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you about two of those night shifts, one in more detail than the other, but if we begin -- if you look to the right there's a screen which I hope will help. Have you had the opportunity to refresh your memory from the notes that you prepared back in November of 2015?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I haven't actually looked at the computer-written notes for a while, but I've had opportunity to read my statement.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: When you made your statement, did you have a look at the notes at that stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Hopefully these will assist you. If we go first to tile 68, please. You mentioned a series of nights.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think you actually cared for [Baby J] on the 25th into 26 November 2015; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If you say so. Looking at my notes --
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Let's have a look at your note and it might, I hope, jog your memory. This is -- in fact, I think it's the note above, thank you. If we look at that first note, 08.07 on 26 November. Does that suggest that was when the note was started on the computer?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. It would have been written retrospectively, so if I was busy on the night shift I would -- when everybody's come on and I can find a quiet corner, I would then write my notes retrospectively for the nights that were done.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: We have heard that the handover would take from 7.30 to 8 and then you would have the opportunity to sit down and make up your notes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: We can see there that in those notes your initials appear, ND.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: And you've entered, speaking of [Baby J] I assume, "Observations stable".
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: "No desaturations."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: "No obvious problems from the stoma fistula."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: "Handles well and has tolerated bag recycling and (inaudible) changes."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And is that:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Has passed urine and bowels opened"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: And:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Fed four-hourly by mum."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: I know you mentioned the parents were helping with cares in the day. Does that suggest that at that stage mum was also helping through the night shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Reads sotto voce.) Reading the notes of the 26th, it says "in the evening", so...
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Let's go on to the next note then if that informs.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You've completed that immediately after the note above.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You finished that at 8.18:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Mummy and daddy did feed and cares together last evening. Mum has provided cares with support from staff overnight."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So mum must have been rooming in that night.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: And, "Happy with the changes put in place yesterday", whatever they may have been?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I can't remember off the top of my head.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: That's the conclusion of your night shift, the 25th into 26 November, and you touched on the next note. Is it right that you handed over to Nurse Ashleigh Hudson for the succeeding day shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If it says so.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: She's completed the next note, we've got the benefit of the notes, but you don't remember?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Okay. You worked a night shift again, did you, on the 26th into 27 November?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Can we go next, please, Mr Murphy, to tile 129? We don't need to go behind that. We've had the benefit of the swipe data. And we understand to enter the neonatal unit you'd swipe a card on the security door and that would admit you. At 9.17 (sic), would that be consistent with type of time you'd turn up for a 7.30 shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, thereabouts.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Move on please to tile 140. We've a representation of the start of that shift (inaudible: coughing) to look at, please. In the top we can see the names of those people who were working, names I suspect you will recognise, but if we can go
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: through them. Dr Brearey and Dr Gibbs were the consultants respectively for the week and on call overnight.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: The registrar and the SHO, we understand they change from time to time, so they may not be -- do you remember either of those as a matter of interest?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Um... no.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Okay. They are again respectively Dr Austin and Dr Verghese. Moving on to the nursing staff, the shift leader that night was Caroline Oakley. As far as registered staff were concerned, Lucy Letby, Mary Griffith and Laura Eagles. Then if we go to the fourth box, we can see there that there were two nursery nurses, yourself and a lady named Vicky Blamire.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Scrolling up again, we can see the allocation of the babies that night if it assists you. Can you see that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you need it enlarged a little bit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I can see.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Importantly for yourself, nursery 4, [Baby J].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You are designated nurse for [Baby J] and a second baby with the initials NW.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we look at the rest of the plan, we can see that Lucy Letby was next door in nursery 3 with two babies.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And again, we can see the rest of the allocations through nursery 1, nursery 2 and a couple of unconfirmed babies. Do you recall being based in nursery 4 that particular evening?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. At the time I gave my first statement I was unsure whether I was in 3 or 4.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Once I'd got over the panic of being interviewed and had chance to reflect, I can confirm that I was in room 4 that night.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Okay. You touched earlier on the stage that [Baby J] had reached in her treatment. What does nursery 4 inform you about that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Nursery 4 usually reflects on a relatively well baby with not complicated -- getting ready for home, not requiring a nurse at her bedside all the time. At night we would add -- I do normal nursery hours, we would put them into the dark and get them ready -- just generally getting them ready for home.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: All right. From the parental note, it seems that mum was helping with some feeding through the night. Would that have been with the same goal in mind?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: All right. We can go next, please, I hope to refresh your memory, to the nursing notes at tile 161. Before we click them, do you have any independent recollection of the shift and how it unfolded with [Baby J]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I do, because I'd had her several times over and on that final night what was unusual for [Baby J] was I wasn't getting much in the way of stuff into her stoma bag for what we call recycling, re-feeding, which was unusual for [Baby J]. She usually had good quantities and we were using able to re-feed the distal stoma quite easily.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: She was growing and doing okay --
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- and I wasn't getting very much in the bag and she was a little bit quieter than normal and I'd already asked the doctors to review her. They said she was okay and to carry on feeding and the night then progressed.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Are you able to recall at what stage of your shift that would have been?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was around and about midnight-ish.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: All right. We'll go to some specific entries that you have made on various forms in a moment but I wonder if we can go to that nursing note, please. Just have a quick look at that, reacquaint yourself, and I'll go through it if I may.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: So:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Observations within normal limits and normal for her pre each feed"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: "Handles well and has woken for each feed. Has taken all feeds very well and settled after each feed."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Then you have made your note:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Nil in bag to recycle at first feed of the shift. Air released and distal stoma redressed as a little bloody."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Is that the type of care that would be required for the stoma on a --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Was that on a regular basis or is that an unusual thing to have to do with a stoma?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It depends, really. Sometimes it's okay, sometimes it just needs a bit more attention. The only thing that was unusual for [Baby J] was on her actual stoma was she had a fistula, so not only was she losing contents from the top of the stoma, she also had a little unusual hole to the side where it joins the skin. So this sometimes made the bag care a little bit difficult because it was making the bag wet where it shouldn't be. So very often the bags would slip or need redressing more frequently than you would normally expect a stoma bag to be redressed because the fistula was causing this to be wet and slippy.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: So you had to presumably have a seal for the recycling bag?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: And that was being interfered with to an extent by leakage from the fistula?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: That was something everyone was aware of and was --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Was that being managed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, and -- well, they decided that she wasn't losing anything internally in her abdomen, that it was all coming out,
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: either across the skin and/or into the bag, so they decided it actually wasn't causing her a problem.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It just meant she was losing from two places.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Then you've noted that there were 33ml to recycle at midnight.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Is that you were saying was a little less than (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I'm about 4 hours adrift.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Right, okay. In what way?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I have said I thought it was about midnight that I didn't get anything. Obviously it was earlier that I didn't get anything and then I had a healthy volume to be able to process and recycle at midnight.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Right, okay. It's between 8 and midnight when you had that concern there wasn't much coming through?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There wasn't as much as normal, but then obviously she's passed some so I've got some to be able to recycle.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: So a more normal situation at midnight?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A more normal amount for her.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: All right. Now, things, I think, moved on because at 4 am you have noted that [Baby J] became unwell after her feed.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: And you have noted there:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Desaturated to the 30s initially."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So is that a very low saturation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's a low number, yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: "Not apnoeic but then required some Neopuff to recover."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: We've heard Neopuff is a delivery of oxygen to help the baby.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Or it's a breath, so it can be with oxygen or air.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Okay. Did you administer that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I will have started it until somebody came to help, yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: And do you remember what was administered?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I said in my statement that I couldn't 100% categorically say that I would have started it but that would be a normal process if you found a baby that required support we would instigate it and call for help at the same time.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, there's no punctuation there and the way that it was put by Mr Astbury reads:
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "[Baby J] became unwell and desaturated to the 30s initially, not apnoeic but then did require..."
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Should it be:
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "Desaturated to the 30s. Initially not apnoeic but then did require some puffs"?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Or what is it? It's not particularly important but do you see the point? Does the "initially" relate to the saturation to the 30s or the apnoea?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm not sure.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm not sure. I wouldn't be using a Neopuff on a baby that was not apnoeic. But I would say maybe she was pausing but hadn't actually gone past the allotted 20-second mark that would trigger it as an apnoea but had dropped her saturations and then had gone on to require Neopuff.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: The point is you Neopuff when the baby's apnoeic and that's what happened here?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, or if she wasn't responding once you'd just touched her -- nudged her to bring her out of whatever episode is happening and if that didn't respond and the saturations remained low we would then use the Neopuff initially with a breath and then, if required, we can add oxygen into that as well.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: So you have put there:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Colour looks poor, pale and mottled."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: That's an observation from 4 am?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: And:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Doctors informed and examined her"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Now, that coincided with a feed at 4 o'clock?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Do you remember whether that feed was completed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not sure. I'd have to look at the feeding chart.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Shall we have a look, please, at this stage the charts that you completed that night. If we can go first to tile 153. These are all in -- these documents we're about to look at are behind divider 13 in jury bundle 2 (inaudible) second one, 16280.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is an observation chart which you will be more than familiar with, I'm sure --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: -- and we're becoming increasingly familiar with.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I want to ask you, please, just about the entries -- we can see the dates across the top and in slightly darker pen we can see entries at 20.00 hours, 24.00 hours, midnight, and 04.00 hours, presumably into the 27th when we look at the dates.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: If we scroll down to the bottom, do you recognise your initials at the bottom of those columns?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Are they the three in the slightly darker pen that I've drawn your attention to?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: So we can see there, if we scroll back up, the general observations of heart rate, moving down, respirations and then temperature. Are the three readings you took all within the parameters that are considered safe and normal?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Scrolling down a little bit more, we can see that [Baby J]'s saturations were 100, 98 and 100 respectively.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we go down a little bit further. We can see, as you pointed out earlier, nil and nil for the recycling at 8 pm when you first came on duty.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: On shift, yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: But then we can see 33 at midnight, as you put in your notes. Then at 4 am, 40. So is that what you would hope to be seeing again?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: All right. You then described [Baby J]'s stools, I think, as loose and yellow; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: You have said "no" as far as a new bag was concerned, that wasn't necessary at that stage. Is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. On my middle one, I'd got some leakage.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There's a Y there. That indicates that there was some leakage. So I obviously hadn't changed the bag, I was obviously able to clean it and contain it.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because we try and change the bag the least amount of times as possible because it irritates the skin.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So if we can not change a bag, it's preferable.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: So that gives us an idea of the stoma care over those 8 hours?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: If we move on, please, to [Baby J]'s feeding chart at tile 142. So that's the 4 am feed which we were dealing with a moment or two ago. Is that your signature on the right-hand side?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It is.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: We've got:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Passed urine and bowels open."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Working our way backwards, the route being B for bottle, is that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: 70ml?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Does that [Baby J] had --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She completed her feed.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Was that completed before she fell ill or did she return to it after the doctors had seen her?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think she had part-way, then was seen, then I was allowed to finish the feed.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: So whatever it was, the doctors were content for her to finish --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: -- what she'd started?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: All right. If we go back, please, to tile 142, we'll just look at the feeding chart for the first part of the shift. I think the last two entries on the right show the 8 o'clock and midnight feeds that [Baby J] was due.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: We can see expressed breast milk, some donor breast milk and some fortifier; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: Feeding normally?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Feeding normally and the -- on the right-hand side, where it says "bowels open", that indicates that the re-feeding of the distal stoma was working well as well because we were actually getting stools in her nappy as well as in her bag.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: There's two parts?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So what we're collecting, what we are re-feeding is obviously going through and going through regularly because she's had her bowels open most nappy cares.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: So despite that concern at 8 o'clock, certainly nothing to cause you to stop feeding [Baby J]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: And things were clearly remedied between midnight and 4 am?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DENNISON

blocks.text: events, a timeline, which also contains the actual notes made contemporaneously.

blocks.text: Sorry, I don't directly remember the events, but from my notes I've put there that I was asked to see the patient, so it wouldn't have been a routine call/visit.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: At that time of day, in a night shift, it would have been because I was asked to attend.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: Let's click behind that tile and go to the doctor's own note. That, you've just described, is the ATSP note, shorthand for "asked to see patient".

blocks.text: Thank you. Moving on through the notes, and we'll consider the entries in your first paragraph that come before the O/E abbreviation for "on examination". In general terms and

blocks.text: knowing your own working practices as I'm sure you do, what would be the source of the information, the data and the description that is in this opening paragraph of yours?

blocks.text: Okay. So everything prior to that OE abbreviation would be a record given by the nursing staff who were present, to kind of relay the most recent events as to why a patient might need seeing or has deteriorated.

blocks.text: So this in effect is the basis on which you were briefed as to the situation --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: -- that caused them to call for you to see patient?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: And were you told therefore, reading through your note, that the patient, [Baby J], had had two profound desats?

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: Then you better describe them individually. The first, to 30s, does that explain the degree to which she desaturated?

blocks.text: I guess there would be objective numbers, but it may not be a true reading, as alluded to in my statement, and on the kind of qualifying criteria of my notes for each desaturation.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: Thank you. I'll invite you to expand on that in a moment. First to 30s:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Being handled during stoma cares."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Two related questions: why would you have noted that it happened while she was being handled due to stoma cares and, secondly, could you expand upon your notion of the true reading or not?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Okay. So the sats monitor is measuring your oxygen levels in the bloodstream. It's an optical probe that has to have good contact with the skin. The machine would normally show you a signal strength to say that you have a good signal. So if there are any movement artefacts or any interference potentially, that desaturation or apparent desaturation on the monitor might not be true, hence it was then potentially trace related. Could there be a bit of doubt that that first desaturation was maybe not a desaturation at all but just because she was moving, wriggling while having her cares done? Could that have been why the monitor alarmed?
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: Picking up on your use of language there, we have on the one hand a true saturation, a true reading, and on the other, I think the phrase you used was a trace related.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: And that is to convey the question of whether or not the probe is properly attached to the baby and therefore providing a reliable and accurate reading of the saturation levels?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. I guess I would say that it's an objective marker, but the second statement where she wasn't handled and then the rest of the clinical history given by the nurses is enough of a clinical concern, regardless of the desaturation, that further steps need to be taken.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: As we've already established, you're receiving this information verbally from the nurse, you weren't present when either of these readings were taken?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: But you're just approaching with a degree of caution because she was being handled at the time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, just that first statement, yes.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: But by way of distinction, the reported second event was a desaturation to the 50s, which in your opinion would seem still profound?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: And on this occasion, you established that the baby, as reported by the nurses, was not being handled at that point?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: And so what conclusions did you draw from that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Again, it could still be trace related. So if the baby moved of her own volition, potentially that could lead to the monitor alarming and saying there was a desaturation, but it's more the things afterwards that probably are definitive -- kind of would give me concern. They said that the nurses had to intervene and give some respiratory support, that the baby was pale and mottled afterwards and was working hard with her breathing. Those are all -- would make me concerned that these were potentially true desaturations. If they were trace related, she should be absolutely fine, she shouldn't have an abnormal colour, she shouldn't be working hard with her breathing, so in
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: the context it probably -- at least one of those was significant.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's continue through the information provided to you. Her heart rate?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that's an abbreviation, HR.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: Take us through that note. Did that attach to the first of the profound desats, the second, both, or aren't you sure?

blocks.text: I assume from my notes it would be from both of the desaturations. The heart rate remaining above 100, I guess, doesn't tell you -- it just shows that they weren't incredibly sick as in peri-arrest. blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: Could you define peri-arrest for us?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Someone who is about to lose cardiac output and then need full CPR, cardiopulmonary resuscitation. So if your body doesn't have enough oxygen, then eventually your heart rate will drop and then fail.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: You then noted, as reported to you, the other indicators that you've told us caused you concern, namely -- what's the first word?

blocks.text: "Since then pale and mottled."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: "Increased work of breathing"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: And you contrasted that, did you, as reported to you, with the presentation prior to these profound desats?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.

blocks.text: You read them to us and tell us what, if any, significance you attach to them.

blocks.text: Thank you. So does that conclude the part of your note that records the information provided to you by the nurses or nurse who had requested your attendance?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: Thereafter do we go to your observations and examination of the baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: How was she?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So based from my notes, rather than recollection of the events, she was alert, her heart sounds -- that's the HS and then it's a diagram for 1 and 2, so normal heart sounds with no murmur. blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: I then proceeded to document my findings of the respiratory examination. That's where then the first kind of abnormalities were detected.

blocks.text: That sign for an arrow upwards and then RR is increased respiratory rate, so she was breathing fast.

blocks.text: Yes. I would say generally, one of the most sensitive markers of someone becoming unwell is that their respiratory
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: markers would go up, would be one of the first things to go. You may be seeing -- you're seeing the start of a decline.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct. So then it's a wee diagram of the tummy. blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: Putting them together, that was a satisfactory examination, was it, or satisfactory results upon examination, I should say?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Of the abdomen, yes. The nursing -- I think it had been noted earlier in the week that she potentially had a fistula, so a small tract that shouldn't be there, in the front of the stoma. blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: So putting all that together, does your next note tell us that you queried the possibility of infection?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: And acting upon that, did you discuss with a Dr Austin — is Dr Austin the registrar at the time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: You discussed with Dr Austin whether or not the baby should undergo a septic screen?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: VERGHESE

blocks.text: And then you set out your plan. Take us through your plan, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So again, [Baby J] was slightly different. Few of our patients would -- because of the recent surgery where she may have then had to be on artificial feeds through her venous system, she had a central line, so it would be a bit of plastic

I can't guarantee that, but there was no clinical reason to take a swab the week before and this particular swab wasn't taken at the time of the desaturations.

blocks.text: What does that mean in language that I can understand?

blocks.text: A Broviac line is a big piece of plastic that goes into a big central vein in the chest and it is tunnelled under the skin, as we saw from the video, to try and reduce infection because central lines are accessed frequently to give drugs or fluids and are at risk of having bugs going from the outside directly into a central line and that's right next to the heart.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: [Baby J] was a well baby. She was ready to go home.

blocks.text: Babies who are ready to go home do not have major desaturations which lead to prolonged resuscitation with Neopuff. They were just unusual for me.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I felt that infection wasn't responsible for that because that isn't the way that infection plays out, and so having looked at other things that may have caused this, I didn't really come to any major conclusion other than these were serious and unexpected deteriorations.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Just in terms of -- just taking you up on your remark that this isn't way that infection normally plays out, in what respect?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, [Baby J] was a patient, because she had the stomas and because she had a Broviac line, who was at risk of infection. But looking at her observation in the days prior to this event, and even on the day of this event, her temperature was stable, her heart rate was stable, her respiratory rate was stable and she was tolerating her feeds. And babies who are kind of brewing an infection tend to exhibit subtle abnormalities in some or all of those things, particularly intolerance of feed, which just shows you that all isn't well, really, and that you need to keep a special watch on them.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And she didn't exhibit any of those things until she had her desaturation, which can be a feature of infection, but then having resuscitated her, she was then better and seemed to be back to normal, that isn't a feature of an infection because by the time she was clinically well and what the medical team have described as back to her normal self, she hadn't even received her antibiotics at that point.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So would you exclude infection as a reasonable cause for what happened to [Baby J]?

blocks.text: Yes, I excluded infection. I don't think that was the cause of her collapse.
